title: If You Retired in 1975, This Is What Life Looked Like

scenes.text: Imagine it's a Friday afternoon in the spring of nineteen seventy-five. You're sixty-five years old. After forty years at the same plant, or the same office, or the same railroad, your coworkers have gathered around a sheet cake. Somebody gives a short speech. Your boss hands you a gold watch. And on Monday morning, for the first time since you were a teenager, you don't have to go anywhere.
scenes.caption: FRIDAY, 1975

scenes.text: If you retired in nineteen seventy-five, you were born around nineteen ten. You remembered the First World War as a child. You came of age during the Great Depression. You probably served in the Second World War, or worked in a factory that built for it. And now, after all of that, you were finally going to rest.
scenes.caption: BORN AROUND 1910

scenes.text: Today, let's look at what that retirement really looked like. Where the money came from, where people lived, what a day was like, and what the world of nineteen seventy-five offered a person who had just finished a lifetime of work. Some of it will sound wonderful. Some of it will sound very hard.
scenes.caption: RETIREMENT IN 1975

scenes.text: In nineteen seventy-five, the gold watch was a real tradition. Many companies gave one after twenty-five or thirty years of service. It was a way of saying thank you, and for many men, it was the most valuable thing they had ever owned. Plenty of those watches are still sitting in dresser drawers today.
scenes.caption: THE GOLD WATCH
scenes.chapter: The gold watch and the pension

scenes.text: More important than the watch was the pension. In the mid-seventies, roughly four in ten private-sector workers were covered by a company pension plan. If you had worked for a big employer, like a steel mill, an auto plant, a utility, the phone company or the government, a check would arrive every month for the rest of your life.
scenes.caption: A CHECK EVERY MONTH

scenes.text: But pensions weren't always safe. When the Studebaker car plant in South Bend, Indiana closed in nineteen sixty-three, thousands of workers lost most of the pension they had been promised. Stories like that led Congress to pass a law called ERISA in nineteen seventy-four, which set rules to protect workers' pensions. For people retiring in seventy-five, it was brand new.
scenes.caption: ERISA, 1974

scenes.text: For most retirees, the most important check was Social Security. And in the seventies, Social Security was growing. Congress raised benefits sharply in the early part of the decade, and starting in nineteen seventy-five, benefits rose automatically with the cost of living every year.
scenes.caption: SOCIAL SECURITY

scenes.text: That mattered enormously, because the seventies were a decade of inflation. In nineteen seventy-four and seventy-five, prices were rising by around ten percent a year. A retiree on a fixed income could watch the price of coffee, meat and gasoline climb month after month. The yearly increase in Social Security kept many people afloat.
scenes.caption: PRICES RISING 10% A YEAR

scenes.text: The results were dramatic. In nineteen fifty-nine, more than one in three Americans over sixty-five lived in poverty. By the mid-seventies, that number had dropped to around fifteen percent. For the first time in American history, growing old no longer meant, for most people, growing poor.
scenes.caption: FROM 1 IN 3 TO 1 IN 7

scenes.text: The other great change was Medicare. It had only been signed into law in July of nineteen sixty-five, by President Lyndon Johnson, at the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri. Harry Truman himself received the very first Medicare card. So if you retired in seventy-five, Medicare was barely ten years old.
scenes.caption: MEDICARE, 1965

scenes.text: Before Medicare, about half of older Americans had no health insurance at all. A single stay in the hospital could wipe out a lifetime of savings. Many older people simply didn't go to the doctor, because they couldn't afford it. By the time you retired in seventy-five, almost every American over sixty-five was covered.
scenes.caption: HALF HAD NO INSURANCE

scenes.text: Medicine itself was still simpler. There were fewer drugs, fewer scans and fewer operations. Heart bypass surgery was still fairly new. Many doctors still made house calls in small towns. And the family doctor who had delivered your children might well be the same one who looked after you in retirement.
scenes.caption: THE FAMILY DOCTOR

scenes.text: Most retirees in nineteen seventy-five stayed right where they were. They lived in the house they had bought in the forties or fifties, and by now, the mortgage was paid off. No rent, no house payment. Just taxes, the electric bill and the heating oil. For many families, the house was the biggest thing they owned.
scenes.caption: THE HOUSE WAS PAID OFF

scenes.text: But a growing number headed south. Florida and Arizona became the great retirement destinations of the decade. Places like Sun City, Arizona, which opened in nineteen sixty, offered golf courses, swimming pools, shuffleboard courts and recreation centers, all designed for people over fifty-five.
scenes.caption: SUN CITY

scenes.text: In Florida, retirees from New York, New Jersey, Ohio and Michigan filled condominiums and mobile home parks from Miami Beach to St. Petersburg. Many of them had spent their whole lives shoveling snow. Now they spent their winters in short sleeves, playing cards by the pool and complaining happily about the humidity.
scenes.caption: FLORIDA

scenes.text: And many retirees lived close to their grown children. It was common for a grandmother to live down the street, or in a little apartment over the garage. Grandparents babysat, cooked Sunday dinners and helped out in a hundred small ways. Families were spread out less than they would be in later decades.
scenes.caption: DOWN THE STREET

scenes.text: So what did a typical day look like? For many retired men, it started early, out of habit. Forty years of punching a clock doesn't go away overnight. Coffee at the kitchen table. The morning paper, read cover to cover. Maybe a walk down to the corner coffee shop, where the same group of retired men met every morning.
scenes.caption: OUT OF HABIT

scenes.text: Then there were projects. Fixing the screen door. Painting the garage. Working in the vegetable garden, which for many retirees was the pride of the summer. Tomatoes, beans, zucchini and more cucumbers than any family could ever eat. The extra went to the neighbors, whether they wanted them or not.
scenes.caption: THE GARDEN

scenes.text: For many women, retirement looked different, because their work at home never stopped. They still cooked, cleaned and kept the household running. But now there was more time for church groups, bridge clubs, quilting circles and volunteering at the hospital. Some said that having their husband home all day was the hardest adjustment of all.
scenes.caption: HER WORK NEVER STOPPED

scenes.text: Afternoons might mean a game of checkers at the senior center, a nap, or a soap opera on the television. In seventy-five, that television probably had about a dozen channels at most, and many towns had only three or four. Evenings meant dinner at five-thirty, the news with Walter Cronkite, and maybe The Lawrence Welk Show on Saturday night.
scenes.caption: DINNER AT 5:30

scenes.text: Getting around in nineteen seventy-five usually meant a big American car. A Buick, an Oldsmobile, a Chrysler or a Cadillac if you'd done well. Long, heavy and comfortable, with a soft ride and a big engine. Many retirees bought one last new car right after the gold watch, and kept it for the rest of their lives.
scenes.caption: ONE LAST NEW CAR

scenes.text: But gasoline had become a worry. The oil embargo of nineteen seventy-three had caused long lines at gas stations, and prices had jumped. By nineteen seventy-five, a gallon of gas cost about fifty-seven cents, almost double what it had been a few years earlier. Some retirees parked the big car and started taking the bus.
scenes.caption: GAS LINES

scenes.text: And retirees discovered travel. Motor coach tours took groups of seniors to see the fall colors in New England, the Grand Canyon or the cherry blossoms in Washington. Some bought a travel trailer or a motor home and spent months on the road. For people who had rarely traveled during their working years, it was a whole new world.
scenes.caption: SEEING THE COUNTRY

scenes.text: What did it cost to live? In nineteen seventy-five, a loaf of bread was about thirty-six cents, a dozen eggs about seventy-seven cents, and a pound of hamburger around eighty-five cents. A first-class stamp was ten cents, and then thirteen cents by the end of the year. A movie ticket cost around two dollars.
scenes.caption: 36 CENTS FOR BREAD

scenes.text: Those numbers sound tiny today, but the average Social Security check for a retired worker was only about two hundred dollars a month. A couple living on Social Security alone had to be careful with every dollar. Clipping coupons, buying day-old bread and saving string were not just habits. They were survival.
scenes.caption: $200 A MONTH

scenes.text: The lucky ones had three legs to stand on. Social Security, a company pension and some savings in the bank, often in a passbook savings account or in United States savings bonds. People called it the three-legged stool. With all three, retirement could be truly comfortable. With only one, it could be very tight.
scenes.caption: THE THREE-LEGGED STOOL

scenes.text: Retirement in nineteen seventy-five wasn't easy for everyone. Many people retired because their bodies simply wore out. Decades in mines, mills and fields left men with bad backs, bad lungs and bad hearts. In the mid-seventies, a man who reached sixty-five could expect to live about another thirteen or fourteen years.
scenes.caption: BODIES WORN OUT

scenes.text: Loneliness was real too. Many women outlived their husbands by ten years or more. Friends moved to Florida or passed away. Children moved to other states for work. Nursing homes were growing fast in the seventies, and some had serious problems with care. For many older people, the fear of ending up in one was very real.
scenes.caption: LONELINESS

scenes.text: And for many, the hardest part was losing a sense of purpose. A man who had been a foreman for twenty years was suddenly just a man at home. Some found new purpose in volunteering, church or grandchildren. Others struggled. Doctors and writers in the seventies started talking openly about the emotional side of retirement for the first time.
scenes.caption: A SENSE OF PURPOSE

scenes.text: And yet, for many people, retirement in nineteen seventy-five was the best time of their lives. They had survived the Depression and the war. They had raised families and paid off their homes. Now they had time, a steady check and a country that had, for the first time, made a real promise to look after its older citizens.
scenes.caption: THE BEST TIME

scenes.text: They had grandchildren to spoil, and many of them did exactly that. Five-dollar bills tucked into birthday cards. Candy in a dish by the door. Fishing trips at the lake. Summer weeks at grandma's house. If you were a child in the seventies, you may remember a retired grandparent who seemed to have all the time in the world for you.
scenes.caption: ALL THE TIME IN THE WORLD

scenes.text: They also had something we've lost a little: community. The same neighbors for thirty years. The same church, the same pew. The same barber, the same diner, the same doctor. When someone was sick, casseroles appeared on the doorstep. Retirement happened in a place where people knew your name.
scenes.caption: PEOPLE KNEW YOUR NAME

scenes.text: Compare that with retirement today. People live longer, often into their eighties and nineties. Most private pensions have been replaced by four-oh-one-k plans, which depend on the stock market. Health care costs far more. And many people keep working well past sixty-five, by choice or by necessity.
scenes.caption: THEN AND NOW

scenes.text: In many ways, the retirees of nineteen seventy-five were the first generation to enjoy a modern retirement, with Social Security, Medicare and a pension all at once. Their parents had mostly worked until they couldn't anymore, then lived with their children. It was a remarkable change in just one generation.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST GENERATION

scenes.text: If you remember a parent or grandparent who retired in the seventies, you remember that world. The gold watch on the dresser. The garden out back. The big car in the driveway. The bowl of candy and the five-dollar bill. They earned every bit of it, and they spent it on the people they loved.
scenes.caption: THEY EARNED IT

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. Who in your family retired in the seventies, and what do you remember about their retirement? And if you're retired today, how does your life compare to theirs? We read every comment. Next time, we're going trick-or-treating in nineteen fifty-eight. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHO RETIRED IN YOUR FAMILY?
